conservation.notes: Endemic to New Zealand. Populations declined considerably after European settlement through habitat loss and predation by introduced mammals, but the species is considered secure and has made local recoveries where livestock and pest control let vegetation recover.

human_tolerance.notes: Tolerates quite small remnant forest patches, regrowth, exotic plantations and well-vegetated suburbs, and is one of the most common birds in urban Wellington. Males aggressively chase other birds, including large ones and raptors, off their feeding trees.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeding is at its height in early spring; Wikipedia places the courtship display flight and the bulk of nesting in September and October. A large untidy cup of twigs, grasses and mosses is built (the female does most of the work), the clutch is usually 4 eggs, the female alone incubates for 14 days, and the chicks fledge after about 20 days.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Both parents feed the fledged young for a further couple of weeks after they leave the nest. Authored judgement on the December-February span, informed by the sourced September-October nesting peak and the sourced post-fledging care period.

phases.name: territorial
phases.note: Authored judgement: outside the breeding window tūī hold and defend favoured nectar and fruit trees, chasing off other birds with loud wingbeats, and follow a local succession of flowering and fruiting plants.

vocalizations.description: A noisy, varied and often soulful song combining bellbird-like notes with clicks, cackles, timber-like creaks and groans and wheezing sounds; different in every individual, and often sung at night around the full moon. The tūī also mimics human speech and other loud sounds it hears.

The harsh, grating calls and loud wingbeats a male uses while chasing other birds off a favoured feeding tree; the calls are described as sounding like rude human speech. Also used as a contact call in flight.

external.note: iNaturalist (P3151), NCBI (P685) and eBird (P3444) ids via Wikidata; GBIF usage key 2487029 matches the GBIF backbone and the ITIS TSN comes from Wikidata P815.

common_names.note: English, French, German and Dutch names from Wikidata P1843. The English name is given without macrons because the IOC World Bird List, which Wikidata follows for English bird names, omits them; 'parson bird' and the Māori name 'koko' are recorded as alternative English names on the same property.

range.note: Endemic to New Zealand: Wikipedia states it is native to New Zealand and found throughout the country including the Chatham, Kermadec and sub-Antarctic Auckland Islands, and Wikidata P183 records New Zealand as the country it is endemic to.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Powered flight is explicitly described ('short wide wings... requiring rapid flapping'); hopping and walking on the ground are included as the ground-foraging gaits the shared program uses.

traits.nest_type.note: 'The large untidy shallow cup-shaped nest is built by both sexes'.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 0.106 kg falls in the Small band.

traits.mass_kg.note: AVONET Mass = 105.83 g (mean of 17 individuals, Mass.Source Dunning), consistent with Wikipedia's nominate-subspecies weights of 65-150 g for males and 58-105 g for females.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 58-150 g, the widest span of Wikipedia's nominate-subspecies figures (females 58-105 g, males 65-150 g).

traits.wingspan_m.note: Honest gap. No openly licensed source consulted (English Wikipedia, Wikidata P2050, AVONET) gives a wingspan for the tūī. Derived from AVONET's mean wing (chord) length of 147.8 mm at a factor of 2.5, giving 0.37 m; a spread wing's span runs roughly two to three times its chord, so treat this as a range estimate rather than a measurement. AVONET's Kipps distance of 29.9 mm on a 147.8 mm wing (ratio 0.20) independently indicates a short, broad wing, which is consistent with a span near the low end of that range.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap: no open-licensed source consulted states a typical or mean wild lifespan for the tūī. 8 years is a judgement for a large, long-lived honeyeater passerine, well below the maximum ages reported for banded birds of its size. Wild figures for honeyeaters this large are rare because banding effort is low.

traits.diet.note: Wikipedia's Feeding section: 'Nectar is the normal diet but fruit and insects are frequently eaten, and pollen and seeds more occasionally.' AVONET independently classifies the species as Trophic.Level Herbivore, Trophic.Niche Nectarivore. Shares are derived from that ordering: nectar 0.55, fruit 0.20, invertebrate 0.20, seed 0.05.

traits.social.note: Wikipedia's Distribution and habitat section: 'Tūī are usually seen singly, in pairs, or in small family groups, but will congregate in large numbers at suitable food sources.' structure Pair reflects the pair-based breeding unit implied by both sexes building the nest and both feeding the young; group_size 1-4 covers singly, pairs and a family group, and deliberately does not span the large feeding aggregations.

traits.defense.note: 'Male tūī can be extremely aggressive, chasing all other birds (large and small) from their territory with loud flapping... They have even been known to mob harriers and magpies.' Mob is the matching defense.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.15, a bold bird. It holds feeding trees against much larger birds and raptors, is one of the most common birds in urban Wellington, and tolerates well-vegetated suburbs, but it does leave a feeding tree when a person closes in.

habitat.use.note: AVONET Habitat = Forest and Primary.Lifestyle = Insessorial; Wikipedia says tūī prefer broadleaf forests at low altitudes and feed in the canopy, hawking insects and gleaning them from tree surfaces. arboreal 0.7 / ground 0.3 reflects that canopy foraging with some ground-level feeding on fallen fruit.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Authored: the nest is built high in the canopy or subcanopy in forest and scrub, so shrub_thicket is the closest available shelter tag.

habitat.resources.note: Feeding and Breeding sections: nectar, fruit, insects, seeds; nest of twigs, grasses and mosses (nest_cup); frequent use of elevated song and lookout perches. Monthly weighting of the fruit and invertebrate shares was left out because no openly licensed source consulted dates the diet's seasonal composition.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Distribution and habitat section: tūī 'will tolerate quite small remnant patches, regrowth, exotic plantations and well-vegetated suburbs' and are 'one of the most common birds found in urban Wellington'. Exploiter is the matching affinity. light_max, impervious_max and flight_distance_m are authored judgements.

seasonal.strategy.note: Wikipedia describes local movement only ('There is much local movement, when tūī follow a seasonal succession of flowering or fruiting plants') and AVONET Migration = 1 (sedentary): the species is a resident, so ActiveYearRound.

seasonal.phases.note: Breeding months, nest structure, clutch size, 14-day incubation, ~20-day fledging and post-fledging care from the Breeding and Behaviour sections, which place the display flight and the main nesting effort in September and October. The end of the young phase and the whole territorial phase are authored judgements from the sourced information on pair-based nesting and year-round defence of feeding trees.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg, altricial nestling (incubated 14 days, fledging at about 20 days) and adult; both sexes feed the young. No sourced duration for the juvenile period was found, so duration_days and scale were left unset rather than guessed.

vocalizations.alarm.note: Songs and calls section for the repertoire ('clicks, cackles, timber-like creaks and groans, and wheezing sounds'); the alarm description is authored from the sourced account of males chasing other birds off a feeding tree with loud flapping and sounds likened to rude human speech.

look.note: Description section for the plumage: near-black head, underparts, wings and tail with a blue-green iridescent sheen, dark reddish-brown upper back and flanks with a bronze sheen, filamentous white feathers on the nape and sides of the neck, two curled white throat tufts (poi) and small white shoulder patches on the upperwing, dark eye and blackish bill and legs. Proportions are authored from AVONET's measurements for this species (culmen 31.3 mm, tarsus 36.5 mm, wing 147.8 mm, tail 118.8 mm, Kipps distance 29.9 mm) read against the biped_winged body plan: a long, slender, slightly decurved bill, a long tail and a short broad wing. wing_aspect is a judgement, since wingspan_m is itself an estimate.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program. food_tag is nectar because nectar is the normal diet; nest_m1/nest_m2 are 9 and 11 for the sourced September-October breeding peak, which the shared program wraps around its hard-coded spring months (so nest-building renders in September and October rather than the full September-January window). flee_m 5 and song_cooldown_s 20 are judgements for a bold, extremely noisy bird.
